title: She should not have been there.
paragraphs: She should not have been there.
That is the part most people skip.

They preach the miracle.
They celebrate the healing.
But they rarely stop long enough to understand what it actually cost that woman to crawl through that crowd and touch the garment of Jesus.
Because according to the Law… she was unclean.

Not emotionally unclean.
Ceremonially unclean.
Socially rejected.
Religiously isolated.
Publicly untouchable.
And for twelve years, her life had become a living funeral.
The story appears in Gospel of Mark 5:25–34, Gospel of Luke 8:43–48, and Gospel of Matthew 9:20–22.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The deeper story begins long before she ever touched His garment.
In the Greek text of Mark 5:25, Scripture says:
“Καὶ γυνὴ οὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος δώδεκα ἔτη…”
“Kai gynē ousa en rhysei haimatos dōdeka etē…”
“And a woman having a flow of blood for twelve years…”
The phrase “ῥύσει αἵματος” (rhysei haimatos) literally means “a continual flowing of blood.”
This was not a temporary sickness.
It was relentless.
And under the Mosaic Law, specifically in Book of Leviticus 15:25–27, a woman with continual bleeding was considered ritually unclean:
“When a woman has a discharge of blood for many days… all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness…”
In Hebrew, the word used is:
“טָמֵא” (tamei)

Unclean.
Defiled.
Separated.

That means everything she touched became ceremonially unclean.
Anyone who touched her became unclean.
Any bed she sat on became unclean.
Imagine this for a moment.

Twelve years without normal human touch.
Twelve years of whispers.
Twelve years of isolation inside crowds.
Twelve years of feeling like God had forgotten her.
God saw it.
You knew what rejection feels like too.

Maybe not in the exact same way.
But you know what it is to carry something that silently destroys you while everyone else keeps moving.
And then Jesus entered the city.
Mark’s Gospel says:
“She had heard the reports about Jesus…”
In Greek:
“ἀκούσασα τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ”
“Akousasa ta peri tou Iēsou”
“She heard the things concerning Jesus.”
Faith often begins that way.

Not with sight.
With hearing.
That is why Epistle to the Romans 10:17 says:
“So then faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”
She heard enough to believe that He was different.

Not merely another rabbi.
Not another religious teacher.

Something in her knew:
If I can just reach Him…
Mark 5:28 records her internal words:
“Ἔλεγεν γὰρ ὅτι…”
“For she kept saying…”

Notice that.
The Greek tense implies repeated speech.
She kept repeating it to herself.
“If I touch even His garments, I will be healed.”
The word for healed is:
“σωθήσομαι” (sōthēsomai)
And this changes everything.
Because this Greek word does not only mean physical healing.

It also means:
saved
rescued
delivered
The same root word is used throughout the New Testament for salvation itself.
She came seeking healing.
But Jesus was about to reveal something greater.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Now notice what she touched.

Most sermons say “the hem of His garment.”
But the Greek says:
“τοῦ ἱματίου αὐτοῦ”
“tou himatiou autou”
His outer garment.
In Jewish context, this likely included the “tzitzit” — the tassels commanded in Book of Numbers 15:38–39.
God commanded Israel:
“Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments…”
The Hebrew word is:
“צִיצִת” (tzitzit)

These tassels represented covenant remembrance.
Obedience.
Holiness.
Identity.
Devout Jewish men wore them as reminders of God’s commands.
And there may be an even deeper prophetic layer here.
In Book of Malachi 4:2, Scripture says:
“But for you who fear My name, the Sun of Righteousness shall rise with healing in His wings.”
The Hebrew word for “wings” is:
“כָּנָף” (kanaph)

It can mean:
wing
edge
corner
extremity of a garment
Many Jewish interpreters connected this prophecy to the corners of the Messiah’s garment.
Read that again.
A bleeding, rejected woman may have reached specifically for the place connected to Messianic healing prophecy.
This was not random desperation.
This was wounded faith colliding with divine mercy.
And immediately…
Mark says:
“καὶ εὐθὺς ἐξηράνθη ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτῆς”
“And immediately the source of her blood dried up.”
The word “πηγή” (pēgē) means fountain or source.

Jesus did not merely stop symptoms.
He shut down the source.
That is what Christ still does.

Religion modifies behavior.
Jesus reaches the root.

Sin is deeper than actions.
It is a condition flowing from the heart.

People try therapy without repentance.
Morality without surrender.
Spirituality without Christ.
But the source remains untouched.
Then something shocking happened.
Jesus stopped.
In a crushing crowd, He asked:
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples almost sounded confused.
Everyone was touching Him.
But not everyone was reaching in faith.
There is a difference between being around Jesus and truly coming to Him.

Church crowds know His name.
Faith touches Him.
And then the woman trembled.
Because now she had to come forward publicly.
Imagine the fear.
According to the Law, she had technically made the crowd unclean by entering among them.

She could have been humiliated.
Condemned.
Rejected again.
But she fell before Him and told “the whole truth.”
That phrase matters.
Because healing and confession are deeply connected throughout Scripture.

Darkness survives in secrecy.
Freedom begins when truth is brought into light.
And then Jesus spoke words no rabbi had likely spoken to her in twelve years.
“θυγάτηρ…”
“Thygatēr…”
“Daughter.”

Not “woman.”
Not “unclean.”
Not “problem.”
Daughter.
The only recorded instance where Jesus directly calls a woman “daughter” in the Gospels.
Do you understand the weight of that?

He restored more than her body.
He restored her identity.
Then He said:
“Your faith has saved you.”
Again, the Greek word is from “σῴζω” (sōzō).

Saved.
Delivered.
Made whole.
This story was never only about blood.
It was about humanity.

Spiritually, we are all unclean before a holy God.
Sin isolates.
Sin corrupts.
Sin separates.
Isaiah 64:6 says:
“All our righteous deeds are like filthy garments.”

The Hebrew imagery there is intentionally severe.
Human goodness cannot cleanse spiritual corruption.
But then Jesus came.
And under the Old Covenant, uncleanness spread by contact.
If you touched the unclean, you became unclean.
But Jesus reversed the flow.
Instead of her uncleanness contaminating Him…
His holiness healed her.
That is the Gospel.

On the cross, Christ took our uncleanness upon Himself.
Our sin.
Our shame.
Our curse.
And in exchange, He gives righteousness, cleansing, and peace to those who come in faith.
You have spent years bleeding internally from things nobody else fully sees.

Secret sin.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
Fear.
Addiction.
Religious hypocrisy.
Hidden despair.
God saw it.
You knew.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus is still stopping for people the crowd ignores.

Still calling broken people “son.”
Still calling shattered people “daughter.”
Still responding to desperate faith.
But you cannot stay hidden forever.
Eventually, like that woman, you must come forward with “the whole truth.”

Not polished religion.
Not image management.
Truth.

Repentance is not humiliation.
It is the doorway where grace enters.
And maybe this story unsettles you because deep down you know you have been close to Jesus without truly touching Him in faith.

You know church language.
You know worship songs.
You know verses.
But you have never surrendered your life.
That woman risked everything to reach Christ.
Most people today will not even risk their pride.

If this pierced something in you, say it plainly.
“No more hiding.”

Someone else reading this is still bleeding silently.
Share this with the person pretending they are fine.
And follow this journey if you want Scripture explained with depth, context, conviction, and the Gospel at the center.
